summary:
Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered aerospace fire safety intelligence platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Transforming complex flight data from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository—including BASS, FLEX/CFI, ACME, SAME/DAFT, and Saffire missions—the system delivers foundational safety insights for deep-space exploration.

Engineered with a Python (Django, DRF, Scikit-Learn) backend and a modern aerospace dashboard, the platform features:

Habitat-Specific Risk Intelligence: Dynamic filtering and ranking across Spacecraft/ISS (0G), Lunar Surface Bases (0.16G), and Martian Habitats (0.38G).

details:
1. What Does It Do or How Does It Work?

Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered aerospace mission control dashboard that digests, ranks, interprets, and models microgravity combustion data from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive. It bridges decades of flight experimentation on the International Space Station (ISS) with actionable engineering protocols for upcoming Artemis Lunar Surface Bases (0.16G), Martian Habitats (0.38G), and Deep Space Transit Vehicles.

Core Architecture & How It Works:

  1. Habitat-Specific Intelligence & Ranking:
    • Evaluates flight data across 5 distinct habitable environments: Space Stations (0G), Spacecraft/Crew Capsules, Lunar Bases (0.16G), Martian Habitats (0.38G), and Pressurized Rovers.
    • Ranks investigations (BASS, FLEX, CFI, ACME, SAME, DAFT, Saffire, SOFIE) based on atmospheric relevance (e.g., elevated O2%O_2\%O2​%, hypobaric pressure, and forced ventilation).
    • Ingests environmental and material parameters (O2%O_2\%O2​%, total pressure, forced ventilation velocity, fuel thickness, fuel phase, diluent gas, and gravity).
      • Combustion Regime (Quenched, Invisible Cool Flame, Steady Hot Burn, Vigorous Spread) with 92%+ classification accuracy.
      • Flame Spread Rate (mm/smm/smm/s) via Gradient Boosting Regression (R2≈0.93R^2 \approx 0.93R2≈0.93).
      • Habitat Fire Hazard Risk Index (0–1000\text{--}1000–100) (R2≈0.93R^2 \approx 0.93R2≈0.93).
    • Detects when ventilation velocities between 3–14 cm/s3\text{--}14\text{ cm/s}3–14 cm/s supply fresh oxidizer faster than convective cooling can extract heat, warning engineers when materials ignite below their 1G Earth Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI).
    • Identifies liquid nnn-alkane droplet vaporization at low temperatures (550–800 K550\text{--}800\text{ K}550–800 K) where visible flames extinguish but invisible cool flames persist.
    • Renders a live 3D Combustion Chamber with orbit/zoom controls, showing the transition from 1G buoyant teardrop soot flames to 0G spherical blue diffusion flames, pulsing cool flame halos, dynamic airflow vectors, and cross-sectional thermal slice planes.
    • Benchmarks flight materials (Kapton HN, PMMA, Nomex III, Silicone, SIBAL fabric) against NASA-STD-6001B Test 1 (upward flame propagation <15 cm<15\text{ cm}<15 cm) and Test 2 (heat/smoke release), dynamically calculating Maximum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) and Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI).
    • A 10 Hz time-series scrubber visualizing real flight sensor curves: d2d^2d2 droplet regression law (mm2 vs smm^2 \text{ vs } smm2 vs s), broadband radiometer heat flux (kW/m2kW/m^2kW/m2), and chamber ΔP\Delta PΔP, pinpointing the millisecond of radiative extinction and cool flame secondary ignition.
    • Generates an executive, printable flight certification dossier detailing habitat ratings, material clearance, and emergency operational rules.

2. What Benefits Does It Have?

  • Removes Data Inaccessibility Barriers: Replaces dense, disparate CSV and video flight logs in NASA’s PSI database with structured visual summaries, intra-investigation comparisons, and downloadable datasets.
  • Prevents Catastrophic Deep-Space Fire Risks: Eliminates dangerous 1G assumptions by explicitly accounting for the absence of natural buoyant convection.
  • Accelerates Spacecraft Materials Certification: Allows mission architects to pre-screen novel composite materials under custom exploration atmospheres (e.g., 34% O2O_2O2​ at 56 kPa) before committing to costly drop-tower or sounding-rocket tests.
  • Optimizes Habitability Life Support Systems (ECLSS): Informs the delicate trade-off between crew cabin pressure/oxygen concentration and material flammability limits.
  • Empowers Cross-Disciplinary Users: Provides tailored interfaces for aerospace safety engineers, academic combustion researchers, and students alike.

3. What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

  • Human Exploration (Artemis & Mars): Deep-space crews cannot simply evacuate to Earth in an emergency. This tool ensures future Lunar and Martian habitats are equipped with predictive fire thresholds, automated damper cutoffs, and tailored suppression protocols.
    • Fine-Water-Mist Fire Extinguishers: Adapts the nitrogen-propelled micro-droplet mist (10–30 μm\mu mμm) developed for the ISS into clean-agent firefighting solutions for terrestrial data centers, lithium-ion battery storage, and historical archives where traditional water or halon causes collateral destruction.
    • SAME / DAFT Optical Pyrolyzate & Dust Sensors: Translates the space station's dual-wavelength optical smoke/dust discrimination instruments into early-warning sensors for mining tunnels, semiconductor cleanrooms, and wildland-urban interface (WUI) communities.
    • Advanced Protective Gear: Highlights flame-resistant polyimide (Kapton) and aramid (Nomex) polymers to improve municipal firefighter turnout jackets and ultralight composite carbon fiber self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA) cylinders.

4. What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use?

  • Backend Architecture:
    • Python 3.13 & Django 5.x: Enterprise web server and robust REST routing.
    • Django REST Framework (DRF): High-performance API endpoints for predictions, audits, telemetry, and live synchronization.
    • Scikit-Learn: Multitask Random Forest & Gradient Boosting models (regime_classifier.joblib, spread_regressor.joblib, risk_regressor.joblib).
    • NumPy & Pandas: Data ingestion, normalization, and microgravity combustion feature engineering.
    • Joblib: Serialized model deployment for low-latency inference (<20 ms<20\text{ ms}<20 ms).
    • Three.js (WebGL): Real-time 3D volumetric combustion chamber, spherical flame deformation, and particle airflow velocity vectors.
    • Chart.js: Interactive 10 Hz flight telemetry time-series replay and habitat parameter distribution charts.
    • HTML5 & Vanilla CSS3/JavaScript (ES6+): Aerospace mission-control UI featuring dark glassmorphism, HUD telemetry panels, and zero external framework bloat.
    • FontAwesome 6 & Google Fonts (Orbitron / Inter): High-contrast aerospace typography.
    • NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) data schema.
    • NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) open citation integration.
    • NASA-STD-6001B Testing Standard specifications.
    • Git & GitHub: Continuous integration and versioning hosted at github.com/bhallapiyush8-svg/nasa-flame.

5. How Is Your Project Creative?

  • Beyond a Static Database Table: Instead of a simple search engine for research papers, we transformed PSI data into an interactive Mission Control flight cockpit.
  • Living 3D Microgravity Physics: Users don't just read about 0G flames—they rotate, slice, and observe the spherical soot-free blue diffusion flame and watch it elongate into a buoyant teardrop as gravity increases from 0G to 1G.
  • Interactive "What-If" Scenario Simulator: Crew members can simulate real-world emergencies (e.g., avionics wire harness electrical fires) and test multi-step mitigations (HVAC damper cutoffs vs. Fine-Water-Mist vs. partial depressurization) to observe real-time damage mitigation percentages.
  • AI Safety Co-Pilot: An intelligent query assistant equipped with NASA PSI flight rules that synthesizes instant physics-backed recommendations for obscure combustion questions.
  • Time-Machine Sensor Replay: Recreating 10 Hz flight telemetry with interactive scrub bars directly visualizes the elusive moment when hot flames extinguish and invisible cool flames ignite.

6. What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

  • NASA Challenge Scope Boundary (Rocket Propulsion Exclusion): We strictly enforced NASA's guideline that rocket engine combustion (u>100 m/su > 100\text{ m/s}u>100 m/s, Richardson number Ri≪10−4Ri \ll 10^{-4}Ri≪10−4) is gravity-independent and therefore excluded. Our modeling focuses exclusively on crew-habitable ambient environments (0–30 cm/s0\text{--}30\text{ cm/s}0–30 cm/s ventilation flow).
  • The 0G Ventilation Paradox: Standard 1G safety logic assumes that reducing airflow reduces fire risk. In microgravity, zero airflow smothers a flame in its own combustion products (CO2/H2OCO_2/H_2OCO2​/H2​O), but gentle cabin drafts (3–14 cm/s3\text{--}14\text{ cm/s}3–14 cm/s) supply fresh O2O_2O2​ while providing insufficient convective heat removal, creating severe low-O2O_2O2​ flammability hazards.
  • Exploration Atmospheres vs. Standard Earth Air: We modeled the specific hypobaric, oxygen-enriched environments planned for the Moon and Mars (e.g., 34% O2O_2O2​ at 56 kPa), where materials ignite faster and burn hotter than in standard ISS cabin air (21% O2O_2O2​ at 101.3 kPa).
  • Intra-Investigation Experimental Hardware Modularity: We explicitly represented how experiments within the same facility differed—such as the ACME project's 6 gaseous flame experiments sharing modular hardware inside the CIR, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) emulating solid/liquid fuel burning using gaseous burners, and the direct hardware reuse between SAME smoke detection and DAFT dust detection.
  • Printable Executive Readiness: We ensured that all complex ML and compliance calculations can be compiled in 1 click into a formal NASA Flight Readiness Dossier suitable for mission flight directors and safety certification boards.
